what_its_for: Filgrastim-aafi helps your body make more white blood cells. White blood cells fight infections. This medicine is used if you have cancer and your white blood cell count is low after chemotherapy, if you have a bone marrow transplant, if you have a chronic low white blood cell count (a condition called severe chronic neutropenia), or if you are donating stem cells for a transplant. It may also be used if you have been exposed to high levels of radiation.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under your skin (subcutaneous) or into a vein (intravenous). Your doctor or nurse will show you how to give yourself the injection at home. Always inject in a different spot each time to prevent soreness. Good places to inject include your belly (at least 2 inches away from your belly button), the front of your thighs, or the upper outer area of your buttocks. Do not shake the syringe or vial. Let the medicine warm to room temperature for about 30 minutes before injecting. Do not use if the liquid looks cloudy or has particles in it.
dosing: Your dose depends on your weight, your medical condition, and why you are taking this medicine. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first. Follow your doctor's instructions carefully about how many days you need to take it.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, call your doctor or healthcare provider right away for instructions. Do not double up on your next dose to make up for the one you missed.
storage: Store this medicine in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. Do not freeze it. If it accidentally freezes, thaw it in the refrigerator once — do not use it if it has been frozen and thawed more than once. You can keep it at room temperature (up to 86°F or 30°C) for no more than 24 hours before using it. Throw away any medicine left in the vial or syringe after use — do not save or reuse it. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of used needles and syringes in a proper sharps container.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting vaccinations without checking with your doctor first. Do not use this medicine within 24 hours before or 24 hours after receiving chemotherapy, as it may not work as well. Avoid touching your face with unwashed hands, and stay away from people who are sick, since your immune system may still be weak.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you have: sudden or severe pain in your upper left belly or left shoulder (this could be a sign of a serious spleen problem), chest pain or shortness of breath (possible lung problem called ARDS), signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing, pain or redness at the injection site that gets worse, signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or unusual tiredness, bone or muscle pain that is severe and not relieved by over-the-counter pain medicine, unusual bleeding or bruising, or swelling in your legs or ankles.
when_it_works: This medicine usually starts increasing your white blood cell count within 1 to 2 days. Your doctor will check your blood regularly to see how well it is working. You may not feel any different, but the blood tests will show your doctor the medicine is doing its job.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of this medicine during pregnancy is not fully known. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits. Children: This medicine can be used in children, but the dose will be carefully calculated by your doctor based on your child's weight and condition. Older adults: Older patients generally use this medicine safely, but your doctor may monitor you more closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your doctor may need to adjust your care plan.
